Q: How to replace the deprecated URL constructors in Java 20? A:

tl;dr

The URI class supplants the legacy class URL.

For a file system path, get a Path object from the Paths utility class from Java NIO.2 in Java 7+. Then convert to a URI object.

Path path = Paths.get( "/Users/your_user_name/example.txt" ) ;
URI uri = path.toUri() ;

Going the other direction, from URI to Path.

Path path = Paths.get( uri ) ;

👉🏽 If you must use the legacy class URL rather than URI, convert.

URL url = Paths.get( "/Users/your_user_name/example.txt" ).toUri().toUrl() ;
  • To construct a URL, use URI::toURL.
  • To construct a relative URL, first create the URI using the context URI and then call URI::resolve with the URI you wish to make relative.
  • To construct a file: based URL, (1) call Path::toURI, (2) then URI::toURL.

Details

Understand that:

  • java.net.URL is an ancient class, dating from Java 1. That class does not encode or decode any URL components according to the RFC 2396 escaping mechanism.
  • java.net.URI class came later, in Java 4.
  • Java NIO.2 arrived in Java 7, bringing the very handy Paths & Files utility classes. (See tutorial.)

Read this note from the Java team, Oracle: Quality Outreach Heads-up - JDK 20: Deprecate URL Public Constructors. To quote:

JDK 20 will deprecate all public constructors of java.net.URL. … To construct a URL, the URI::toURL alternative should instead be preferred. To construct a file: based URL, Path::toURI should be used prior to URI::toURL.

And see the note on constructor deprecation within the Javadoc of the URL class.

See also the issue-tracker page, JDK-8294241 Deprecate URL public constructors.

Example: File path URI

For working with files in modern Java, use NIO.2 features.

  1. The Paths class can produce a Path object.
  2. From there, ask that Path to produce a URI.
Path path = Paths.get( "/Users/your_user_name/example.txt" ) ;
URI uri = path.toUri() ;

uri.toString() = file:///Users/your_user_name/example.txt

Going the other direction:

Path path = Paths.get( uri ) ;

Convert from URI to URL

The question asks for the legacy class URL. If you must have a URL object to interoperate with old code not yet updated to the URI class, you can convert.

URL url = uri.toUrl() ;

Q: I have this problem with mongoDB and node.js A:

That ECONNREFUSED error with the _mongodb._tcp prefix is a classic. It essentially means your Node.js application is trying to find your MongoDB cluster, but something is blocking the handshake or the address itself isn't resolving correctly.

1. The "Whitelisting" Check (Most Common)

MongoDB Atlas has a firewall. Even if your username and password are correct, Atlas will reject the connection if your current IP address isn't on the "Allowed" list.

  • Go to MongoDB Atlas.

  • In the left sidebar, click Network Access.

  • Click Add IP Address.

  • Click Add Current IP Address (or, if you are just testing and moving around, choose "Allow Access from Anywhere," though this is less secure).

  • Wait about 30–60 seconds for the status to turn "Active" and try running npm run dev again.

2. The Connection String Format

Your URI looks like a standard SRV string: mongodb+srv://...

Sometimes, certain network configurations (like some VPNs or strict home routers) struggle with the +srv protocol.

Try this:

In MongoDB Atlas, when you click Connect > Drivers, look for the option to use an older driver version (e.g., Node.js 2.2.12 or later). This will give you a "Standard Connection String" that looks like this:

mongodb://myuser:mypassword@cluster0-shard-00-00.mongodb.net:27017,...

Replace your .env string with that longer version and see if it connects.

3. Special Characters in Passwords

If your password contains special characters like @, :, or /, it will break the URI because those characters have specific meanings in a URL.

  • Fix: Either change your database user password to use only alphanumeric characters, or URL-encode the special characters (e.g., @ becomes %40).

4. Node.js & DNS Issues

The error querySrv ECONNREFUSED often means your machine is failing to look up the DNS SRV record.

  • Quick Test: Try changing your computer's DNS settings to Google's DNS (8.8.8.8) or Cloudflare (1.1.1.1).

  • Alternative: Ensure you don't have a VPN or a work firewall active that might be blocking port 27017 or DNS SRV lookups.

A Small Code Suggestion

In your server.js, you are calling connectDB() inside the app.listen callback. While this works, it’s usually better to connect to the database before starting the server to ensure you don't start accepting requests before the "brain" (the database) is ready.

JavaScript

// Optimized order
const startServer = async () => {
    try {
        await connectDB();
        app.listen(5000, () => {
            console.log('Server started at http://localhost:5000');
        });
    } catch (error) {
        console.log("Failed to start server:", error);
    }
};

startServer();
